questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Compute magnitude of a gradient vector
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: f(x,y)=x^2+y^2; gradient at (1,2) is <2,4>; magnitude?
questions.explanation: Magnitude is the square root of the sum of squared components, so |<2,4>| = sqrt(4 + 16) = sqrt(20), about 4.472. Adding components to get 6 confuses magnitude with a plain sum.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: f=x^2+y^2, grad at (1,0)=<2,0>, unit u=<1,0>; directional derivative?
questions.explanation: The directional derivative is the dot product of gradient with the unit direction: <2,0> dot <1,0> = 2. Using the gradient's magnitude 4 ignores that u points only along x.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: positive divergence at a point indicates?
questions.explanation: Positive divergence means net outflow. B reverses; C zero; D curl.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: F=<y, -x>; curl (scalar) = ∂Q/∂x - ∂P/∂y = -1 -1 =?
questions.explanation: For F = <P,Q> the scalar curl is dQ/dx - dP/dy. Here d(-x)/dx = -1 and d(y)/dy = 1, so the curl is -2; expecting 0 overlooks that both contributions are negative.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: line integral of F along C with respect to arc length uses?
questions.explanation: Line integral uses F·T ds. B normal; C drops direction; D omits dot.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line integral with respect to y
questions.learningObjective: Set up line integral with respect to y
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: C: x=t, y=t, t 0 to 1; ∫ x dy = ∫ t*dt? value?
questions.explanation: Write dy = y'(t) dt = dt and x = t, turning the integral into ∫_0^1 t dt = 1/2. Taking the integrand as 1 or skipping the parameterization gives 1.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line integral with respect to x
questions.learningObjective: Set up line integral with respect to x
questions.stem: Along the line x=t, y=t for 0<=t<=1, evaluate the line integral of y with respect to x.
questions.explanation: Here dx = x'(t) dt = dt and y = t, so the integral is ∫_0^1 t dt = 1/2. Treating y as the constant 1 ignores how it changes along the path.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line integral with respect to arc length
questions.learningObjective: Compute line integral with respect to arc length
questions.stem: For the diagonal path x=y=t with t running from 0 to 1, compute the line integral of 1 with respect to arc length.
questions.explanation: The arc length element is ds = sqrt(x'^2 + y'^2) dt = sqrt(2) dt, so the integral is sqrt(2), about 1.414. Using dt instead of ds gives 1 and misses the path's speed.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Compute work as line integral of force
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: F=<1,0>, path from (0,0) to (2,0); work?
questions.explanation: Work is ∫ F·dr; along the x-axis dr = <dx,0>, so F·dr = dx and the integral from 0 to 2 equals 2. Answering 0 ignores that the force pushes along the direction of motion.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: circulation of F around closed curve C is?

options.text: Double integral of F over region
options.misconception: uses a double integral, which gives flux-type quantities, not circulation

options.text: Line integral of F·dr around C

questions.explanation: Circulation is the line integral of the tangential component around a closed curve, ∮ F·dr. A double integral of a vector field is not scalar circulation, and divergence measures net outflow rather than swirl.
questions.hint: Circulation is line integral around closed curve.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Compute curl of a vector field
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: F=<P,Q> in 2D; curl = ∂Q/∂x - ∂P/∂y. If P=y, Q=x, curl?
questions.explanation: dQ/dx - dP/dy = d(x)/dx - d(y)/dy = 1 - 1 = 0. Adding the partials to get 2 confuses curl, which subtracts, with divergence, which adds.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Use Green's theorem to compute area
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: area = (1/2) ∮ (x dy - y dx). For square 0 to1: value?
questions.explanation: The area formula is (1/2)∮(x dy - y dx); for the unit square it returns the geometric area 1. Doubling to 2 forgets the factor 1/2 in the formula.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: ∫_0^1∫_0^2 (x+y) dx dy? compute (integrate x 0-2, y 0-1).
questions.explanation: Integrating x from 0 to 2 gives 2, then adding 2y and integrating y from 0 to 1 adds 1 for a total of 3. Treating the inner result as a constant 2 and dropping the y term gives the wrong 2.5.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: changing integration order can simplify when?

options.text: When inner integral is hard but outer becomes easy

questions.explanation: Order change helps when inner becomes tractable. B denies; C overstates; D restricts.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: ∫_2^0 1 dx =?
questions.explanation: Reversing limits negates an integral, so ∫_2^0 1 dx = -∫_0^2 1 dx = -2. Reporting +2 ignores the orientation encoded in the bounds.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Polar coordinates for a double integral
questions.learningObjective: Set up double integral in polar
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: area of quarter circle radius 2 in polar: (1/2)∫_0^{π/2}∫_0^2 r dr dθ? value?
questions.explanation: The inner integral ∫_0^2 r dr is 2, and sweeping theta from 0 to pi/2 multiplies by pi/2 to give pi, about 3.1416. Using 2pi would cover a full circle instead of a quarter.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Angular range in a polar integral
questions.learningObjective: Choose angular range for a full circle
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: full circle in polar requires θ range?

options.misconception: uses 0 to pi, which traces only half the circle

questions.explanation: A polar curve completes a full circle only when theta sweeps 2pi radians. Ranges 0 to pi and -pi/2 to pi/2 cover half circles, and 0 to pi/2 covers only a quarter.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: volume of unit cube via ∫∫∫ dV =?
questions.explanation: Volume is ∭ dV over the region; for the unit cube it is 1*1*1 = 1. Adding the side lengths to get 3 confuses the count of dimensions with the volume.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Apply fundamental theorem for line integrals
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: if F=∇f, ∫_C F·dr = f(B)-f(A). For f=x^2, path (0) to (2): value?
questions.explanation: For a gradient field the integral depends only on endpoints: f(2) - f(0) = 4 - 0 = 4. Integrating the coordinate x from 0 to 2 gives 2, which is not the potential difference.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Recognize work is path independent in conservative field
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: in a conservative field, work between two points is?
questions.explanation: Conservative fields have path-independent work. B reverses; C closed loop; D unbounded.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: for a parametric curve, curvature formula involves?

options.misconception: treats an area quantity as relevant to the turning rate of a curve

questions.explanation: Curvature can be written as |dT/ds|, which for a parametric curve involves velocity, speed, and acceleration, including derivatives of the speed. Position alone or acceleration alone cannot capture how quickly the tangent turns.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: gradient points in direction of?

options.misconception: uses the negative gradient, which points toward steepest decrease

questions.explanation: The gradient points toward steepest increase because the directional derivative grad·u is largest when u aligns with grad. Its negative gives steepest decrease, and the level-curve tangent is perpendicular to it.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: divergence measures outflow; curl measures?

options.misconception: picks speed, which describes motion rather than a field's local rotation

questions.explanation: Curl measures local rotation or circulation density, while divergence measures net outflow. Gradient and speed describe different aspects of fields and motion.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Recognize a field with nonzero curl cannot be gradient
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: a vector field with nonzero curl cannot be?

options.misconception: calls it a divergence field, but curl and divergence are independent operators

questions.explanation: Every gradient field has zero curl because mixed partials commute, so a field with nonzero curl cannot be conservative. Zero and constant fields are separate cases.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: Jacobian for polar coordinates is?

options.misconception: treats the area element as dr dtheta, ignoring radial stretching
uses r^2, which overcounts the polar cell area
uses 1/r, the inverse of the actual Jacobian factor

questions.explanation: The polar area element is r dr dtheta, so the Jacobian is r, accounting for arc length growing with radius. Omitting, squaring, or inverting r misstates how polar cells scale.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: a field is path independent on simply connected domain if?

options.misconception: uses nonlinearity, which has no bearing on path independence

questions.explanation: On a simply connected domain zero curl is equivalent to a conservative field, which makes line integrals path independent. Constant magnitude and zero divergence do not imply that.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Choose between shell and disk method
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: shell method integrates along axis parallel to?

options.misconception: describes a direction unrelated to shell construction
uses tangency to the curve, not how shells are oriented

questions.explanation: Cylindrical shells are built parallel to the axis of rotation, so integration runs along the perpendicular coordinate. The disk method instead uses slices perpendicular to the axis.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: Green's theorem requires region to be?

options.misconception: chooses disconnected, the opposite of the required connected region
chooses infinite, though Green's theorem needs a bounded region
chooses point-like, a degenerate region with no area

questions.explanation: Green's theorem needs a region with piecewise smooth boundary and, in its basic form, simple connectivity. Disconnected, infinite, or point-like regions fail those hypotheses.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: positive orientation of boundary keeps region?

options.misconception: uses 'behind you', which is not part of the orientation convention

options.text: On the left as you traverse

options.misconception: uses 'above you', which does not define an orientation

questions.explanation: Positive boundary orientation traverses the curve so the region stays on the left, which is counterclockwise for a simple closed curve. Keeping it on the right reverses orientation and flips the integral's sign.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: F=<3,4> constant; curl?
questions.explanation: All partial derivatives of a constant field are zero, so dQ/dx - dP/dy = 0. Multiplying the components 3 and 4 to get 12 confuses curl with a product.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: magnitude of gradient equals?

options.misconception: picks the minimum rate, which the negative gradient gives

options.text: Maximum rate of change of f

questions.explanation: The directional derivative equals grad·u, which is largest when u points along the gradient, so |grad| is the maximum rate of change. It is not a minimum, an average, or always zero.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: gradient operates on scalar field; divergence operates on?

options.misconception: claims divergence works only on constants, but it applies to any differentiable vector field

questions.explanation: Gradient maps a scalar field to a vector, while divergence maps a vector field to a scalar. Divergence is not restricted to constants and is not an operation on tensors at this level.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: zero curl everywhere on simply connected domain implies?
questions.explanation: Zero curl ⇒ conservative (simply connected). B divergence; C constant; D zero field.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: path-independent integral implies the field is?

options.misconception: picks non-conservative, the opposite of path independence

questions.explanation: On a simply connected domain path independence is equivalent to a conservative field, the gradient of a potential. It therefore has zero curl rather than nonzero curl, and being divergence-free is a different property.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: why does the polar Jacobian r appear in area integrals?

answer.exemplar: The Jacobian r accounts for the fact that area elements grow with radius, converting dx dy to r dr d theta.

questions.explanation: Jacobian r converts Cartesian area to polar. A slip says it is arbitrary.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: f=x+y+z; gradient? x-component?
questions.explanation: The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives, <1,1,1>, so its x-component is 1. Reporting 3 confuses the number of variables with the value of one partial derivative.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: f=x^2+y^2, grad at (1,1)=<2,2>; direction angle degrees? (45)
questions.explanation: The vector <2,2> has equal components, so it points along the line y = x, at 45 degrees from the positive x-axis. A 90-degree answer would require a vertical vector.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: F=<0, x, 0>; curl z-component = ∂Q/∂x - ∂P/∂y? with Q=x,P=0 => 1. value?
questions.explanation: The z-component of curl is dQ/dx - dP/dy = d(x)/dx - d(0)/dy = 1 - 0 = 1. Reporting 0 misses that Q varies with x.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: nonzero curl at a point indicates?

options.misconception: picks zero area, which says nothing about local rotation

questions.explanation: A nonzero curl at a point measures local rotation or circulation density. Net outflow is divergence, steepest increase belongs to the gradient, and zero area is unrelated.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line integrals with respect to arc length
questions.learningObjective: Compute line integral wrt arc length
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: C unit circle, ∫ 1 ds = circumference?
questions.explanation: Integrating 1 with respect to arc length gives the curve's total length; for the unit circle that is the circumference 2pi, about 6.283. Getting 2 confuses circumference with diameter.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: f=x^2+y^2, grad at (0,0)=<0,0>; magnitude?
questions.explanation: At the origin the partial derivatives of x^2 + y^2 are both zero, so the gradient is <0,0> and its magnitude is 0. This is a critical point; reporting 1 confuses the coordinates with the gradient.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Compute directional derivative in arbitrary direction
questions.stem: Using f(x,y)=x^2+y^2 with gradient <2,0> at (1,0), find the directional derivative in the direction u=<0,1>.
questions.explanation: With gradient <2,0> and unit direction <0,1>, the dot product is 2*0 + 0*1 = 0. The function has no first-order change in the y direction there.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: F=<x,y>; divergence = 1+1 =?
questions.explanation: Divergence is dP/dx + dQ/dy = d(x)/dx + d(y)/dy = 1 + 1 = 2. Getting 0 would require subtracting, which is the rule for curl.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: F=<y,x>; curl = ∂x/∂x - ∂y/∂y = 1-1 =?
questions.explanation: Scalar curl is dQ/dx - dP/dy = d(x)/dx - d(y)/dy = 1 - 1 = 0. Adding to get 2 confuses curl with divergence.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: line integral with respect to x uses integrand?

options.misconception: uses F·n ds, the flux integrand, rather than a component times dx

questions.explanation: A line integral with respect to x uses the component P(x,y) times dx; it is not the vector line integral F·T ds nor the flux form F·n ds. Those involve the unit tangent or normal with a different measure.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line integral with respect to y
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: C: x=t, y=t^2, t 0 to1; ∫ x dy = ∫ t*2t dt = 2∫t^2 dt? value?
questions.explanation: 2∫_0^1 t^2 dt = 2/3 ≈0.6667. A slip gives 2/3? same; slip gives 1.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line integral with respect to x
questions.stem: On the parabolic arc x=t, y=t^2 for 0<=t<=1, evaluate the line integral of y with respect to x.
questions.explanation: Since dx = x'(t) dt = dt and y = t^2, the integral is ∫_0^1 t^2 dt = 1/3, about 0.3333. Using y = t or skipping the dx conversion gives a wrong result.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line integral with respect to arc length
questions.learningObjective: Compute arc length of a path
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: path x=t,y=t, t 0 to1; arc length =?
questions.explanation: ds = sqrt(x'^2 + y'^2) dt = sqrt(2) dt, integrated from 0 to 1 gives sqrt(2), about 1.414. Getting 2 comes from adding the coordinate changes instead of taking the square root of squared rates.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Compute work for a non-constant force
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: F=<x,0>, path (0,0) to (2,0); work = ∫_0^2 x dx =?
questions.explanation: Along the x-axis F·dr = x dx, so work is ∫_0^2 x dx = 2. Getting 4 treats the force as constant at its endpoint value.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Compute circulation for a simple field
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: F=<-y,x>, unit circle; circulation = 2π? value?
questions.explanation: By Green's theorem the circulation equals the double integral of curl, which is 2, over the unit disk of area pi, giving 2pi, about 6.283. Reporting 2 forgets to multiply by the area.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: F=<y,0>; curl = ∂0/∂x - ∂y/∂y =?
questions.explanation: dQ/dx - dP/dy = d(0)/dx - d(y)/dy = 0 - 1 = -1. Dropping the negative sign gives 1 and ignores the order of subtraction.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: triangle (0,0),(1,0),(0,1) area via Green =?
questions.explanation: The triangle has base 1 and height 1, so its area is 1/2, and the Green's theorem line integral returns that same area. Reporting 1 uses the enclosing square's area.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: ∫_0^2∫_0^3 1 dxdy =?
questions.explanation: Integrating 1 over a rectangle gives its area; dimensions 3 by 2 give 6. Adding the side lengths to get 5 confuses area with a sum of dimensions.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: ∫_0^1∫_0^y 1 dxdy =? (region x≤y)
questions.explanation: The region 0<=x<=y<=1 is a right triangle with area 1/2. Treating it as the full unit square gives 1 and ignores the x<=y constraint.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: ∫_1^0 x dx =?
questions.explanation: Reversed limits flip the sign, so ∫_1^0 x dx = -∫_0^1 x dx = -1/2. Reporting +0.5 ignores the direction of integration.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Polar coordinates for a double integral
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: area semicircle radius 1 = (1/2)∫_0^π∫_0^1 r dr dθ =?
questions.explanation: The polar integral gives (1/2)*(theta range pi)*(inner result 1/2) = pi/2, about 1.5708, half the unit disk's area pi. Reporting pi treats the region as the full disk.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Angular range in a polar integral
questions.learningObjective: Compute polar area of quarter circle
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: quarter circle radius 1 area = (1/2)∫_0^{π/2}∫_0^1 r dr dθ =?
questions.explanation: (1/2)*(pi/2)*(1/2) = pi/4, about 0.7854, one quarter of the unit disk area pi. Reporting pi/2 would be a semicircle's area.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Compute triple integral of constant over box
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: ∫_0^1∫_0^2∫_0^3 1 dxdydz =?
questions.explanation: Integrating 1 over the box gives its volume, 3*2*1 = 6. Adding the side lengths to get 5 confuses volume with a sum of dimensions.

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.stem: Legal clerk note: f=x^2+y^2, from (0,0) to (1,1): f(B)-f(A)=?
